deep.reconstruction:
WHAT THE PAGE IS. Each block heading 'p.h' pairs a prime p with a number h. All thirteen primes on the page (1613, 1597, 1549, 1493, 1453, 1429, 1381, 1373, 1301, 1277, 1237, 1229, 1213) satisfy p ≡ 5 (mod 8). Together they are exactly the primes ≡ 5 (mod 8) between 1200 and 1620. The previous page treats the primes 1621–1933 of the same type, so this is part of a run through the second thousand.

h is the number of properly primitive classes of binary forms of determinant D = −p, in Gauss's convention (a,b,c) with b² − ac = D. In modern terms h = h(−4p). Because p ≡ 5 (mod 8), h ≡ 2 (mod 4) and there is a single nonprincipal ambiguous class J = (2,1,(p+1)/2).

HOW EACH TABLE IS BUILT. Gauss picks a form g = (q,b₁,c₁) that generates the class group. Usually q is the smallest suitable prime with −p a square mod q, e.g. (3,1,(p+1)/3) for 1613, 1493, 1373, 1301, 1277 and 1229. When the smallest such prime does not generate, he takes another form:
- (11,3) for 1597;
- (10,1) for 1549, 1429 and (10,3) for 1381;
- (26,9) for 1453, because (13,·) has only order 7 there;
- (7,3) for 1237;
- (23,11) for 1213, because (13,10) = g² has order 5 there.

Row k lists a form 'a.b' in the class g^k. Here b² ≡ −p (mod a), b is determined only up to sign and modulo a, and the forms are not always reduced. In 1373 he writes the full triples 27.25.74 and 17.2.81. Each step composes the previous form with g. When q divides a, the composition partly cancels; for example, in 1613, (39,8) = (3,−1)(13,8), so g^6 = (13,8,129).

Worked example for 1613 (my verification):
- (81,13,22) ~ (22,9,77) = g⁴.
- (22,9)(3,1) = (66,31,39) ~ (39,8,43) = g⁵.
- g⁶ = (13,8,129), g⁷ = (39,34), g⁸ ~ (14,5,117), g⁹ = (42,19,47), g¹⁰ = (17,6,97), g¹¹: a = 34.

HOW THE ORDER IS FOUND (stopping rule). Composing with J takes the class of a form a′ to the class of 2a′. Hence g^(h/2 − k) = J·g^(−k) has first coefficient 2·a_k, after reduction. As soon as a row k+j shows a = 2·a_k with matching b, Gauss reads off h/2 = 2k + j. The rows are numbered 0…h/2, and the tail rows can be filled in at once. The cases:
- 1613: 17 → 34 at rows 10, 11, so h/2 = 21 and h = 42.
- 1597: 34, 17 at rows 3, 4, so 7 and 14. Tail: row 5 = J·g^(−2), with (82,65,71) ~ (23,…), giving 23; then 22 = 2·11; then 2.
- 1549: 38, 19 at rows 4, 5, so 9 and 18.
- 1493: 22 at row 4 vs 11 at row 7, so 11 and 22. Tail: 18, 6, 2 = 2·9, 2·3, 2·1.
- 1453: 34, 17 at rows 3, 4, so 7 and 14. Tail: 31 from (74,29,31), 13 from 26/2, then 2.
- 1429: 34 at row 5, 17 at row 6, so 11 and 22. Tail: 11, 13, 31, 5, 2.
- 1381: 17, 34 at rows 6, 7, so 13 and 26. Tail: 37 from (38,5,37), 26, 22, 31, 5, 2.
- 1373: 17, 34 at rows 4, 5, so 9 and 18. Tail: 18, 6, 2.
- 1301: 30.7 at row 12 vs 15.8 at row 13; 10.7 vs 5.3; 30.17 vs 15.13. All give h/2 = 25, so h = 50.
- 1277: 7.2 at row 7 vs 14.5 at row 10, so 17 and 34.
- 1237: 34, 17 at rows 3, 4, so 7 and 14. Tail: 19, 14, 2.
- 1229: 15.4 at row 9 vs 30 at row 10, and 5.4 at row 8 vs 10 at row 11, so 19 and 38.
- 1213: 2 at row 5, so h = 10.

STATISTICS BOX.
- '13. 50.42.38.34.26.22.22.18.18.14.14.14.10': the 13 class numbers sorted in decreasing order. Their sum is 322, and the mean is 322/13 = 24 10/13.
- '28. 840. 30': cumulative with the previous page, which had 15 primes and sum 518 (mean 34 8/15). So 28 primes, sum 518 + 322 = 840, mean 30.
- The next page continues: 8 primes with sum 224, giving 36 primes and 1064 in total. Its 'Chil.' summary lists 36 · 1064 · max 70 for the second chiliad (1000–2000).

PURPOSE. This is Gauss's empirical tabulation, by chiliads, of class numbers for negative determinants −p with p ≡ 5 (mod 8). It tracks counts, sums, means and maxima, in service of his asymptotic mean-value statements on class numbers (Disq. Arith. art. 302) and of his class-number tables. It also shows the group is cyclic, since a single form has order h.
errors: 1301.50, row 8: as transcribed, '13.9' is impossible, since 81+1301 = 1382 is not divisible by 13. The correct form is 13.5 (25+1301 = 1326 = 13·102). Either the glyph is a 5 or it is a slip of the pen.

1597.14, row 2: '41.34' is impossible (1156+1597 = 2753 is not divisible by 41). The correct form is 41.24 (576+1597 = 2173 = 41·53, and 24² ≡ 2 ≡ −1597 mod 41). The digit is overwritten in the manuscript.
Several entries are valid forms but not reduced, e.g. 13.8 for 1613 (reduced would be 13.−5) and 27.25.74 for 1373. This is intentional working notation, not an error.
No arithmetic errors found in the sums: 322 = 13·24 + 10, 518 + 322 = 840, 840/28 = 30.

results.what: Class numbers of binary forms with determinant −p, i.e. h(−4p), for the 13 primes p ≡ 5 (mod 8) between 1213 and 1613: 42, 14, 18, 22, 14, 22, 26, 18, 50, 34, 14, 38, 10. Each is found as the order of a generating form, computed by repeated composition and reduction.
results.modern_name: Class group computation via powers of a prime form (baby-step order finding in a cyclic class group Cl(−4p))
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Disquisitiones Arithmeticae 1801, arts. 305–306; class-number tables published posthumously in Werke II)

results.what: Shortcut for the order: since J·[a′] = [2a′] for the ambiguous class J = (2,1,(p+1)/2), seeing a = 2·a_k at row k+j gives h/2 = 2k+j. The second half of the cycle then follows without further composition.
results.modern_name: Using the 2-torsion (genus/ambiguous class) to halve an order computation

results.what: Sums and means of class numbers over primes ≡ 5 mod 8 in the second chiliad: 13 primes, sum 322, mean 24 10/13; running total 28 primes, sum 840, mean 30.
results.modern_name: Empirical average order of class numbers (precursor of the Gauss–Lipschitz–Mertens mean-value results / Dirichlet class number formula averages)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Disq. Arith. art. 302, conjectural mean values; chiliad tables in Werke II)

deep.surprise_reason: These are working sheets for Gauss's well-known chiliad tables of class numbers of negative determinants, made with his standard composition method. The statistics fit his known empirical study of average class numbers. Nothing here goes beyond what is documented in Werke II.
